content: Silica gel is a granular, porous form of silica that is synthetically produced from sodium silicate. Despite its name, silica gel is actually a solid material. It is most commonly encountered in everyday life as small beads packaged in semi-permeable plastic sachets. These sachets are used as desiccants to control local humidity and prevent spoilage of various goods. Due to the presence of potentially toxic dopants and its high moisture absorption capacity, silica gel packets are typically labeled with warnings advising against ingestion. If consumed, pure silica gel is unlikely to cause acute or chronic illness but may still pose risks. However, some desiccant packets may contain fungicides or pesticides, which may not always be explicitly labeled. Food-grade desiccants, on the other hand, are not expected to include harmful poisons that could cause long-term harm if consumed in the small quantities typically found in food packaging. Silica gel was patented in 1919 by Walter A. Patrick, a chemistry professor at Johns Hopkins University. During World War I, it was used in gas mask canisters to absorb vapors and gases. The material itself, however, dates back to the 1640s as a scientific curiosity. In World War II, silica gel played a critical role in the war effort by keeping penicillin dry, protecting military equipment from moisture damage, serving as a fluid cracking catalyst for producing high-octane gasoline, and acting as a catalyst support for the production of butadiene from ethanol, which was essential for synthetic rubber manufacturing. Silica gel has a high surface area, approximately 800 m²/g, which allows it to readily absorb water. This property makes it an effective desiccant or drying agent. Once saturated with water, silica gel can be regenerated by heating it to 120°C (250°F) for two hours. Certain types of silica gel may pop when exposed to sufficient water. Silica gel is widely used as a desiccant in various applications. It helps prevent mold growth and spoilage in items such as leather and food products like pepperoni. It also protects electronics and slows the decomposition of chemicals, such as those in vitamin pills, by reducing moisture. Silica gel sachets are often added to these items to extend their shelf life. In high-frequency radio or satellite transmission systems, silica gel is used to maintain low relative humidity inside waveguides, preventing moisture buildup that could cause arcing or signal interference. In industrial compressed air systems, silica gel is employed to dry the air, preventing damage caused by condensation or moisture. This same principle is applied in railway locomotives to prevent brake failure due to ice or condensation in brake air pipes. Additionally, silica gel is used in museums and libraries to control relative humidity in exhibitions and storage areas. In the field of chemistry, silica gel is commonly used as a stationary phase in chromatography. In column chromatography, silica gel particles (typically 40-63 μm in size) are used due to their polarity, which causes non-polar components to elute before polar ones in normal-phase chromatography. When hydrophobic groups, such as C18 groups, are attached to the silica gel, the method becomes reverse-phase chromatography, where polar components elute first. Silica gel is also applied to aluminum or plastic sheets for thin-layer chromatography. Chelating groups can be covalently bound to silica gel, enabling the selective removal of metal ions from aqueous solutions. These chelating groups can also be grafted onto silica gel surfaces using polyamines, resulting in materials with enhanced mechanical integrity. Silica gel can also be combined with alkali metals to form M-SG reducing agents. Silica gel is sometimes used as cat litter, either alone or in combination with traditional materials like clays, including bentonite. It is virtually odorless, does not track, and is effective, though it tends to be more expensive than other options. Silica gel, in its pure form, is non-toxic, non-flammable, and chemically inert. However, some silica gel beads are doped with moisture indicators, such as cobalt(II) chloride, which is toxic and potentially carcinogenic. Cobalt(II) chloride appears deep blue when dry and turns pink when hydrated. While crystalline silica dust can cause silicosis, synthetic amorphous silica gel is non-friable and does not pose this risk. A related material with significantly greater porosity is aerogel.
